```{r setup}
#| include: false
source(here::here("package_demo.R"))

library(ggplot2)
library(prefio)
library(prefviz)
library(dplyr)
library(plotly)
library(kableExtra)
library(tibble)
```

## Imagine you are a club president, and you want to figure what drinks to order for the next major events...

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%" .fragment}
So you make a list of drinks, and go out to ask every member to rank their preference from most to least preferred.

1. Coke
2. Orange juice
3. Coffee
:::

::: {.column width="50%" .fragment}
After everyone has made their choice, your data looks like this:

```{r}
#| echo: false 

# Define the people and drink types
people <- c("Alice", "Ben", "Carla", "David", "Ella")
drinks <- c("coke", "orange juice", "coffee")

# Create the tibble with random rankings for illustration
set.seed(123)  # for reproducibility

df <- expand.grid(name = people, drink_type = drinks) %>%
  group_by(name) %>%
  mutate(rank = sample(1:3, size = length(drinks), replace = FALSE)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  as_tibble()

df
```

:::
::::

## You decided to look into people's first choice

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%" .fragment}
Coffee seems to be the most popular drink among the people, followed by coke and orange juice.
```{r}
composition_tbl <- tibble(
  coke = 0.30,
  `orange juice` = 0.20,
  coffee = 0.50
)

kable(composition_tbl)
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%" .fragment}
Which can be visualized easily with a bar chart or a stacked bar chart
```{r}
composition_long <- composition_tbl %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "drink", values_to = "percentage")

# Create stacked bar chart
ggplot(composition_long, aes(x = 1, y = percentage, fill = drink)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(percentage, "%")), 
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5), 
            color = "white", fontface = "bold", size = 4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("coke" = "#FF6B6B", 
                               "orange juice" = "#FECA57", 
                               "coffee" = "#8B4513")) +
  labs(title = "Drink first preference")  +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "right",
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 14, face = "bold"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 12))
```

:::
::::

## What if you run the same poll in all 4 Monash campuses?

Visualizing the data is a bit more challenging, but it's still possible to see the differences between the campuses.
```{r}
composition_tbl <- tibble(
  campus = c("Clayton", "Caulfield", "Peninsula", "Parkville"),
  coke = c(0.70, 0.20, 0.10, 0.05),
  `orange juice` = c(0.10, 0.60, 0.15, 0.25),
  coffee = c(0.20, 0.20, 0.75, 0.70)
)

composition_long <- composition_tbl %>%
  pivot_longer(-campus, names_to = "drink", values_to = "pct")

ggplot(composition_long, aes(x = campus, y = pct, fill = drink)) +
  geom_col(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(pct, accuracy = 1)), 
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5), 
            color = "white", fontface = "bold", size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("coke" = "#FF6B6B", 
                               "orange juice" = "#FECA57", 
                               "coffee" = "#8B4513")) +
  labs(y = "Proportion", title = "Drink Preferences by Campus") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "right",
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 14, face = "bold"),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent)
```

## But what if you run this poll across all university campuses in Australia?

I don't know how many campuses there are in Australia, but assume 150 campuses 😬😬😬

```{r}
#| fig.width: 10
#| fig-align: center

set.seed(42)
n_campuses <- 150

# Generate 150 campus compositions (same diverse patterns as 4-campus example)
composition_tbl <- tibble(
  campus = paste0("Campus_", 1:n_campuses),
  coke = runif(n_campuses, 0.05, 0.80),
  `orange juice` = runif(n_campuses, 0.05, 0.80),
  coffee = 1 - coke - `orange juice`
) %>%
  mutate(across(coke:`orange juice`, ~ pmax(pmin(., 0.90), 0.05))) %>%
  mutate(coffee = 1 - coke - `orange juice`) |> 
  filter(coffee > 0, coke > 0, `orange juice` > 0)

# Same 4-campus style plot, now for 150 campuses
composition_long <- composition_tbl %>%
  pivot_longer(-campus, names_to = "drink", values_to = "pct")

ggplot(composition_long, aes(x = campus, y = pct, fill = drink)) +
  geom_col(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(pct, accuracy = 1)), 
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5), 
            color = "white", fontface = "bold", size = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("coke" = "#FF6B6B", 
                               "orange juice" = "#FECA57", 
                               "coffee" = "#8B4513")) +
  labs(y = "Proportion", title = "Drink Preferences: 150 Campuses") +
  theme(legend.position = "right",
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 14, face = "bold"),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, size = 3),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 6))
```

## Introduce: Ternary plot 🎉🎉🎉

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}



![](abcnews.png)

*ABC News shows interesting plot on 2025 House of Rep's distribution of first preference*
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

**How to read this plot?**

::: {.incremental}
- The edges are the axes, running from 0 to 1
- Each point represents 1 observation (or stacked bar), and is made up of 3 parts: %ALP, %LNP, and %Other
- If the point sits at one of the vertices, it means 100% of the composition is in that party.
- If the point sits in the center, it means equal compositions of all party (33% each)
:::

:::

::::

## We make it interactive!

Hover to see electorate names and exact vote percentages.
```{r p2d_interactive}
#| echo: false

p2d_interactive
```

## We make it interactive!

**Explore with map of electorate**

Link the ternary plot with a map of electorates. Selecting a point in the ternary plot highlights the corresponding electorate on the map, and vice versa.

```{r linked_map}
#| echo: false

bscols(
  widths = c(4, 8),
  plotly_ternary,
  plotly_map
)
```
